caption_and_notes: Table 1. Fertilizer-use targets and prediction agreement across countries Values in parentheses are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Valid n is the number of profiles with observed nitrogen rates; each country contained 70 sampled profiles. Pearson correlations and paired conventional-model comparisons used adoption-stratified profile bootstraps. Ensemble nitrogen-quantity errors are predicted minus observed quantities in kg N per eligible plot; their intervals used joint post-stratum bootstraps with fixed weights. The prevalence pool is broader than the post-stratification target pool. Adoption targets for Ethiopia and Niger are not directly comparable with those for other countries (Section 2.5).

Table 2. Higher-use versus lower-use country-label contrasts Higher-use labels are Ethiopia, Malawi and Nigeria; lower-use labels are Niger, Tanzania and Uganda. Mali is excluded. Contrasts use the same 70 Tanzanian profiles; values in parentheses are 95% bootstrap intervals stratified by observed adoption. Post-stratified contrasts use fixed profile weights. Expanded quantities apply only to eligible weighted plot records. All p values refer to unweighted contrasts. Provider p values come from paired t tests with Holm adjustment across the three providers within each outcome. Ensemble p values are unadjusted and descriptive; the ensemble is not a fourth independent provider. kt N means thousand tonnes of nitrogen.

Table 3. Distribution and concentration of ensemble label contrasts Results describe the 70 Tanzanian profiles. Positive contrasts are the percentage of profiles with a positive rate contrast within each group. Expanded contrasts are paired rate differences multiplied by plot area and post-stratification weight. The top-10 and top-20 rows rank profiles by their contributions, from largest to smallest. Groups overlap, so shares should not be added across grouping schemes. Shares are rounded percentages of the net contrast. Quartiles refer to observed plot area; kt N means thousand tonnes of nitrogen. An em dash indicates that a statistic is not reported for that group.

Table S1. Study components and comparisons. Benchmarks compare predictions with observed fertilizer use; the paired experiment tests sensitivity to country labels. Survey weights and plot areas convert rate contrasts into nitrogen-quantity scenarios. Profiles describe plot managers and their cultivated plots.

Table S2. Fertilizer-use indicators and observed nitrogen rates. The frozen fertilizer indicator defines the sampling and adoption groups. A positive nitrogen rate is a quality-controlled rate > 0. Zero and missing rates among indicator-positive profiles were retained; no indicator-negative profile had a positive rate.

Table S3. Structured model outputs and internal consistency. Records include the benchmark, ablation and seven-label analyses. The survey quality-control threshold of 300 kg N ha⁻¹ is used here only to check model output ranges; outputs were not truncated. Supplementary Table S4 documents response reuse and retries.

Table S4. Response collection, reuse and retries. Analysis records are experiment-tagged rows; each accepted response is assigned to its first collection phase. On 26 August, profile blocks and three arm positions were randomized (seed 20260826). On 27 August, the seven-label manifest was randomized (seed 20260827), but only five labels were newly queried. Tanzania and Nigeria responses were reused after prompt-hash verification. The matrix therefore spans collection stages; matching hashes do not establish identical runtime conditions. Retries for reused rows are included in the ablation row and are not counted twice in the total. Overall, 3,570 analysis records represent 3,150 distinct accepted responses; four conditions required five extra attempts, with one accepted response retained per condition.

Table S5. Additional validation metrics and household-cluster sensitivity. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) measures how well adoption scores distinguish users from non-users. The Brier score is the mean squared error between an adoption score and observed adoption; MAE is mean absolute error. Adoption AUC and Brier scores use all 70 profiles per country. The 'Valid / positive N' column counts valid and positive observed nitrogen rates. Rate and quantity metrics require valid observed rates; positive-user metrics include only rates > 0. Confidence intervals use 10,000 within-country profile bootstraps stratified by observed adoption, except the final column, which uses household-cluster resampling. Constant adoption scores yield AUC = 0.500 when both classes are present; correlations are undefined (NA) for constant rate predictions. A constant no-adoption prediction has an invariant Brier score under adoption-stratified resampling.
columns: Positive-user N-rate MAE(kg N ha⁻¹; 95% CI)

caption_and_notes: Table S6. Predictor sets and model fitting for the conventional transfer benchmarks. The predictor sets are not nested: country and administrative-location category appear only in matched inputs, while rich inputs add other survey covariates. Hurdle and constrained random-forest models are selected separately for each target country using source-country data only. Imputation, standardization and encoding are fitted within each source-country training split and applied to validation or target records.

Table S7. Paired differences in correlations between conventional models and the LLM ensemble. Delta r = conventional r − LLM ensemble r. The 95% confidence intervals use 10,000 adoption-stratified bootstrap draws, resampling the same profiles for both methods. Each specification has seven exploratory country comparisons without multiplicity adjustment. Comparisons use the paired differences, not overlap between the two methods’ separate intervals.

Table S8. Predictions and errors from the national-statistics benchmark. Panel (a) lists country values; panel (b) summarizes errors. National fertilizer use is based on FAO data reported by the World Bank (indicator AG.CON.FERT.ZS; kg N + P₂O₅ + K₂O per ha of arable land), averaged over the survey year and adjacent years. Regression predictions use leave-one-country-out OLS fits of the survey target on that statistic, truncated at zero for rates and to [0, 1] for adoption. LLM values are post-stratified ensemble predictions with 95% intervals from 10,000 adoption-stratified profile bootstraps with weights fixed. Primary rate targets exclude plot rates above 300 kg N ha⁻¹; capped targets limit those rates to 300 kg N ha⁻¹. †Adoption targets are not comparable with those for the other countries (Section 2.5). The analysis is exploratory.

Table S9. Trait associations in survey data and LLM predictions. Coefficients come from regressions on eight traits with country fixed effects. Survey models used all area-eligible plots with complete traits (63,099 plots for N rate; 64,045 with capping; 64,917 for adoption) and household survey weights. Their 95% intervals used 500 cluster bootstraps within countries. Groups combined country and enumeration-area identifiers; records missing enumeration-area identifiers instead used country and household identifiers. LLM models used ensemble predictions for 488 profiles, with 95% intervals from 2,000 within-country profile bootstraps. Survey cross-validation used five folds with the same groups; prediction cross-validation used ten folds. Resampling and cross-validation used seed 20260827. Nitrogen-rate coefficients are in kg N ha⁻¹. Adoption coefficients are proportion-point differences in observed binary adoption or mean predicted adoption; age is per 10 years, and plot and farm size are per doubling. For adoption, traits explained 3.3% (survey) and 39.2% (LLM) of within-country variation out of sample; the ratio of summed absolute LLM to survey coefficients was 3.01. Signs agreed for 20 of 26 country × trait coefficients clearly non-zero in the survey. For N rate, the corresponding explained shares were 3.0% (survey) and 39.2% (LLM), and the absolute-coefficient ratio was 1.17. Signs agreed for 18 of 25 country × trait coefficients clearly non-zero in the survey. For capped N rate, the shares were 4.2% (survey) and 39.2% (LLM), and the ratio was 0.81. Signs agreed for 17 of 23 country × trait coefficients clearly non-zero in the survey. These analyses are exploratory. Ensemble adoption is the fraction of three providers predicting use, not a calibrated individual probability. The profile and survey samples have different distributions. Coefficients outside survey intervals are descriptive comparisons, not formal tests of coefficient differences. Household grouping does not cover dependence between households in unidentified enumeration areas (Supplementary Text S4). Missing inorganic-fertilizer responses were coded as non-use; Table S10 reports complete-case sensitivity.

Table S10. Sensitivity of observed adoption associations to missing responses The exploratory adoption model coded 398 missing inorganic-fertilizer responses as non-users. Complete-case analysis excluded these records, retaining 64,519 plots versus 64,917 in the primary model. All eight coefficient signs were unchanged. The largest absolute coefficient change was below 0.00010, equivalent to 0.01 percentage points. This comparison concerns point estimates; no new confidence intervals were calculated.

Table S11. Post-stratification weights and effective sample sizes. Post-strata combine the fertilizer-use indicator, manager sex and formal education. Kish effective n = (sum of weights)² / sum of squared weights; CV is the coefficient of variation. Maximum weight share is the largest profile weight divided by the country total. These diagnostics describe each weighted sample of 70 profiles, not the full survey design.

Table S12. Predictions under the East Africa and Tanzania labels. Results use 70 Tanzanian profiles. Paired differences have 95% intervals from 10,000 adoption-stratified profile bootstraps. Rank correlations compare profile rankings between the two label conditions.
